title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT during science investigation tasks. The central question is whether students can effectively formulate prompts, evaluate AI-generated answers, and decide when to continue or stop asking follow-up questions in an AI-mediated learning activity.

The study is not an instructional intervention or reading/literacy experiment; rather, it is an observational study of student behavior while using ChatGPT 3.5 in a structured task-based setting. Sixty-three French students aged 14–15 from four schools completed six science problems. For each problem, they were shown either an efficient or inefficient suggested prompt, could use it or write their own prompt, interacted freely with ChatGPT, and rated each response they received. The researchers analyzed prompt discrimination, answer-evaluation sensitivity, follow-up behavior, and final written explanations, along with relationships to metacognition, prior knowledge, and attitudes toward AI.

Results showed consistently weak performance: students were near chance at distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts, often rated low-quality AI answers as useful, and rarely asked follow-up questions even after unsatisfactory responses. Final task success was only moderate, and better outcomes were associated with receiving more high-level AI answers, being more sensitive to answer quality, and asking follow-up questions. Positive AI attitudes and higher self-reported prior knowledge were associated with poorer regulation, while metacognitive regulation and critical perceptions of AI were protective. The authors conclude that students need explicit AI literacy and metacognitive scaffolding to avoid over-reliance and the illusion of understanding.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot, used for generating and evaluating natural-language responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM in six middle-school science investigation tasks; students prompted ChatGPT, evaluated its responses, and optionally asked follow-up questions.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of n=63 middle-school students, prompt-quality discrimination was at chance level (mean d'=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08), indicating that students could not reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts for ChatGPT. Students also accepted inefficient prompts 75.9% of the time after judging them as inefficient.
findings.measure: Signal detection sensitivity for prompt-quality discrimination (d')

findings.finding_summary: Students showed near-zero ability to evaluate ChatGPT answer quality (mean d'=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). They rated 71.4% of expert-coded low-level answers as clear/useful, and only 16 students exceeded 70% evaluation accuracy.
findings.measure: Signal detection sensitivity for answer-quality discrimination (d')

findings.finding_summary: Behavioral regulation was weak: only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions, totaling 22 follow-up questions across six tasks. Even after low-level answers, students initiated follow-up only 31.8% of the time, suggesting premature termination of QA cycles.

Task outcomes were modest overall: the average correct solution rate across six problems was Msuccess=0.51 (SD=0.25). The best-fitting model predicted success rate from the frequency of high-level answers received (beta=0.52, p=0.000), answer-evaluation sensitivity (beta=0.1, p=0.000), and follow-up questioning after low-level answers (beta=0.4, p=0.004); adjusted R2=0.81, F(5,57)=40.29, p<0.0001.
findings.measure: Final written explanation accuracy / conceptual understanding

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical study with a clear within-subjects design, but it is observational/correlational rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison against a control condition. It provides useful descriptive evidence about ChatGPT use in middle-school learning, but not causal literacy-instruction effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported effects are on interaction quality and task success, with moderate associations in the regression model (e.g., beta=0.52 and beta=0.4) but no direct instructional effect size against a comparison group. Overall, the paper shows negative or null evidence about students’ ability to use ChatGPT effectively rather than positive learning impact.
